member.summary: Storage-agnostic file management implementation targeting Amazon Simple Storage Service (AWS S3) and S3-compatible providers. Manages files using S3 object keys and streams data directly via the AWS S3 client without local disk staging for reads. Writes are buffered to disk via a local storage service in the temporary directory before streaming to S3 to minimize memory overhead for large files. Thread-safe for singleton lifecycle across concurrent and parallel asynchronous tasks.

para.b: Architectural Rationale: Disk Spooling vs. In-Memory Buffering

remarks.para:
High-throughput computational workloads—such as experimental data segmentation, numerical model simulations, and parametric sweep exports—frequently generate datasets exceeding tens or hundreds of megabytes. Buffering outgoing payloads entirely in RAM (e.g., via ) introduces severe reliability and scalability vulnerabilities:
O(1) vs. O(N) Space Complexity & Memory Cost Efficiency: Storage disk (NVMe/SSD) is orders of magnitude less expensive per gigabyte than physical RAM. By spooling data to the OS-managed temporary directory, memory allocation per active write stream remains strictly constant (O(1), governed by the underlying page buffer of 64KB–128KB), regardless of whether the generated artifact is 1 MB or 50 GB. In contrast, in-memory buffering scales linearly (O(N)) with file size and concurrent requests, precipitating catastrophic (OOM) failures under high concurrency.
Garbage Collection & Large Object Heap (LOH) Protection: In the .NET runtime, continuous byte array expansions in dynamically growing in-memory streams cross the 85,000-byte threshold, landing directly on the Large Object Heap. Because the LOH is not compacted during Generation 0 or 1 GC sweeps, dynamic in-memory buffering induces chronic memory fragmentation and forces expensive, blocking Generation 2 collections (Stop-the-World pauses). Disk spooling completely bypasses LOH allocations during generation.
Producer-Network Decoupling & Latency Resilience: Writing to local disk decouples data generation from WAN throughput. The application writes at local bus speeds (GB/s via the OS page cache) without stalling on cloud network latency or TCP windowing. Intermittent network degradation or slow transmission rates do not block compute threads. Furthermore, long simulation steps that experience delays between successive writes do not risk HTTP socket idle timeouts against the AWS S3 API.
Transactional Fault Isolation & Zero-Leak Lifecycle: If a failure occurs during file calculation or data serialization, the partial artifact remains local and is safely cleaned up, preventing orphaned partial objects or corrupted versions in the S3 bucket and avoiding wasteful AWS API PutObject costs. Upload transmission triggers only upon stream completion (), and the enclosing finally block guarantees deterministic destruction of both the temporary file and its isolated upload partition directory.

member.name: T:MelloSilveiraTools.Core.Managers.File.Providers.BlobStorage.BlobStorageFileStorageService
member.summary: Storage-agnostic file management implementation targeting Azure Blob Storage and Azure-compatible providers. Manages files using blob names and streams data directly via the Azure Blob Storage client without local disk staging for reads. Writes are buffered to disk via a local storage service in the temporary directory before streaming to Azure Blob Storage to minimize memory overhead for large files. Thread-safe for singleton lifecycle across concurrent and parallel asynchronous tasks.

para.b: Architectural Rationale: Disk Spooling vs. In-Memory Buffering

remarks.para:
High-throughput computational workloads—such as experimental data segmentation, numerical model simulations, and parametric sweep exports—frequently generate datasets exceeding tens or hundreds of megabytes. Buffering outgoing payloads entirely in RAM (e.g., via ) introduces severe reliability and scalability vulnerabilities:
O(1) vs. O(N) Space Complexity & Memory Cost Efficiency: Storage disk (NVMe/SSD) is orders of magnitude less expensive per gigabyte than physical RAM. By spooling data to the OS-managed temporary directory, memory allocation per active write stream remains strictly constant (O(1), governed by the underlying page buffer of 64KB–128KB), regardless of whether the generated artifact is 1 MB or 50 GB. In contrast, in-memory buffering scales linearly (O(N)) with file size and concurrent requests, precipitating catastrophic (OOM) failures under high concurrency.
Garbage Collection & Large Object Heap (LOH) Protection: In the .NET runtime, continuous byte array expansions in dynamically growing in-memory streams cross the 85,000-byte threshold, landing directly on the Large Object Heap. Because the LOH is not compacted during Generation 0 or 1 GC sweeps, dynamic in-memory buffering induces chronic memory fragmentation and forces expensive, blocking Generation 2 collections (Stop-the-World pauses). Disk spooling completely bypasses LOH allocations during generation.
Producer-Network Decoupling & Latency Resilience: Writing to local disk decouples data generation from WAN throughput. The application writes at local bus speeds (GB/s via the OS page cache) without stalling on cloud network latency or TCP windowing. Intermittent network degradation or slow transmission rates do not block compute threads. Furthermore, long simulation steps that experience delays between successive writes do not risk HTTP socket idle timeouts against the Azure Blob Storage API.
Transactional Fault Isolation & Zero-Leak Lifecycle: If a failure occurs during file calculation or data serialization, the partial artifact remains local and is safely cleaned up, preventing orphaned partial objects or corrupted versions in the blob container and avoiding wasteful Azure Storage API transaction costs. Upload transmission triggers only upon stream completion (), and the enclosing finally block guarantees deterministic destruction of both the temporary file and its isolated upload partition directory.

Uses for buffer management to reduce GC pressure

Growth strategy optimized for both small and large string scenarios
Ref struct implementation ensures stack-only semantics

Cannot be used as a field in classes or non-ref structs
Cannot be boxed or stored in heap-allocated collections
Cannot cross async method boundaries (including lambda captures)

Append(ReadOnlySpan): ~1 cycle per character (vectorized)
Growth operations: O(n) but minimized by growth strategy
